prompt: Which family does a sequence diagram belong to in UML?
hint: Does it show what exists, or what happens?

choices.text: Behaviour, as one of the interaction diagrams
choices.why: Right: it shows what happens over time, and sits with communication, timing and interaction overview diagrams.

choices.text: Structure, because it lists the participants of a system
choices.why: It names participants, but what it shows is messages in time order, which is behaviour.

choices.text: Neither; it was added to UML by C4
choices.why: Sequence diagrams are part of UML itself. C4 borrows from UML, not the other way round.

choices.text: Deployment, since its lifelines are machines
choices.why: Lifelines can be anything that sends or receives messages; deployment is a separate structure diagram.

prompt: The course says it uses UML as sketch. What does that mean for a diagram you draw?
hint: Partial is not the same as careless.

choices.text: It can use the symbols loosely, since sketches are informal
choices.why: A reader who knows UML reads the symbols you drew; a diamond on the wrong end still says the opposite.

choices.text: It needs to be complete enough to generate code from
choices.why: That is UML as programming language, the third mode.

choices.text: It shows only what the question needs, with each mark used correctly
choices.why: Yes: partial in scope, exact in notation.

choices.text: It should be detailed enough for a contractor to build from
choices.why: That is UML as blueprint.

prompt: This is the lesson's use case diagram with its words removed. Put each name on the part it belongs to.
hint: The arrow with a hollow head joins two actors.

prompt: Applying a coupon is optional when buying a ticket. How is that drawn, and which way does the arrow point?
hint: The base use case does not know about the optional one.

choices.text: «include», from buy a ticket to apply a coupon
choices.why: Include is for behaviour the base always uses; a coupon is optional.

choices.text: «extend», from apply a coupon to buy a ticket
choices.why: Right: the extension points at the base use case it may add to.

choices.text: «extend», from buy a ticket to apply a coupon
choices.why: The direction is reversed: extend points from the optional behaviour to the base.

choices.text: A solid arrow, since the coupon comes before the payment
choices.why: A use case diagram has no time in it; order belongs in an activity or sequence diagram.

prompt: Which of these are mistakes the lesson names in use case diagrams? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four were numbered in the wrong diagram.

choices.text: A use case called Login screen
choices.why: Yes: a screen is a step, not a goal an actor would recognise.

choices.text: Arrows between use cases showing their order
choices.why: Yes: there is no time in a use case diagram.

choices.text: The booking database drawn as an actor
choices.why: Yes: it is inside the system, and actors are outside by definition.

choices.text: The payment gateway drawn as an actor
choices.why: That one is right: the gateway is outside Carcará's system, a supporting actor.

prompt: These are the six relationship lines of a class diagram with their names removed. Put each name on its line.
hint: Look at the end of each line and whether it is dashed.

prompt: The diagram shows Booking 1 —— 1..* Ticket with a filled diamond beside Booking. What does it claim?
hint: Read multiplicity from the far end; the diamond sits on the whole.

choices.text: A ticket may belong to several bookings at once
choices.why: The 1 beside Booking says each ticket belongs to exactly one booking.

choices.text: A booking owns one or more tickets, which end with it
choices.why: Right: composition on the booking's side, at least one ticket per booking.

choices.text: A ticket owns its booking
choices.why: That would put the diamond beside Ticket; the diamond marks the whole.

choices.text: A booking may exist without tickets, and a ticket without a booking
choices.why: 1..* means at least one ticket, and the 1 means a ticket always has its booking.

prompt: In UML multiplicity, a passenger who may have no loyalty card or exactly one is written ___.
hint: A lower bound, two dots, an upper bound.

prompt: Ticket carries bookingId: Long, and a line also joins Ticket to Booking. What is wrong?
hint: In a class diagram, what is the line?

choices.text: The attribute is fine; it documents the line for readers who skim
choices.why: It says the same thing twice, and the second time in the database's terms.

choices.text: It should be bookingId: String
choices.why: The type is not the problem; the attribute is.

choices.text: It says the reference twice, once as a column
choices.why: Yes: that is the schema in disguise.

choices.text: Composition forbids attributes on the part
choices.why: Parts have attributes like any class. The problem is this one duplicates the association.

prompt: A draft draws Trip as a composed part of Ticket. Using the lesson's numbers, what would that claim mean at São João?
hint: What happens to a composed part when its whole is deleted?

choices.text: Cancelling one ticket would delete a shared departure
choices.why: Right: a composed part ends with its whole, and a trip is shared by every ticket on it.

choices.text: Each ticket would need its own bus
choices.why: Composition says nothing about buses; it is about ownership and lifetime.

choices.text: The trip would have to keep a list of the tickets sold for it
choices.why: That is navigability, a separate decision drawn with arrowheads.

choices.text: Little, as composition is a sketch-level detail
choices.why: It is a precise claim about lifetime, and a reader who knows UML will take it literally.

prompt: Match each mark of a sequence diagram to what it means.
hint: Filled waits; open does not.

pairs.right: a synchronous message: the sender waits
an asynchronous message: the sender carries on

right_distractors: a class the message belongs to

prompt: Why does Carcará's purchase hold the seat in a request of its own, before the payment?
hint: What must never happen to a passenger?

choices.text: Because the payment gateway is synchronous
choices.why: Being synchronous is about waiting, not about the order of hold and charge.

choices.text: So nobody pays for a seat somebody else got first
choices.why: Yes: the seat is held before any money moves.

choices.text: To make the diagram easier to read
choices.why: The order is a decision about the system, and the diagram shows it.

choices.text: Because Redis refuses calls after a payment
choices.why: Nothing stops that call; the order exists to protect the passenger.

prompt: Using the lesson's p95 times — 120 ms to the API, 1,400 ms for the card charge, 8 ms for the database write and 120 ms back — roughly how many milliseconds does the passenger wait for the payment?
hint: A synchronous chain waits for the sum.

prompt: The API's call to the payment gateway times out. Why is calling again, without anything else, dangerous?
hint: What was lost: the charge, or the answer?

choices.text: The seat hold would be lost
choices.why: The hold lasts ten minutes and is unaffected by a retry.

choices.text: The gateway forbids retries
choices.why: Gateways accept retries; the question is whether a retry is recognised as the same charge.

choices.text: If the first charge went through, a retry charges twice
choices.why: Right: a timeout loses the answer, not necessarily the charge. The idempotency key makes the retry safe.

choices.text: The booking database would end up holding two bookings for the seat
choices.why: The booking was written once, before the payment; the risk is on the card.

prompt: The app gives up on the API after 5 seconds; the API gives up on the gateway after 30. What does the lesson say happens?
hint: Who stops waiting first?

choices.text: The API keeps working on a request nobody is waiting for
choices.why: Yes: the inner timeout should be shorter than the outer one, and here it is not.

choices.text: The passenger sees the result after 30 seconds
choices.why: The app stopped waiting at 5 seconds; it never receives the answer.

choices.text: The gateway cancels the charge at 5 seconds
choices.why: The gateway knows nothing about the app's timeout.

choices.text: No harm, as long as both timeouts exist
choices.why: Their order matters as much as their existence.

prompt: On a component diagram, a socket has no ball fitted to it. What does that tell you?
hint: A socket is a requirement.

choices.text: The component provides an interface no other part uses
choices.why: That would be a ball with no socket.

choices.text: A requirement nothing provides
choices.why: Right: a gap, either in the diagram or in the system, and it is worth finding out which of the two.

choices.text: The component is deployed on its own
choices.why: Components say nothing about where they run.

choices.text: The interface is asynchronous
choices.why: Ball and socket say nothing about timing.

prompt: Otávio asks whether Carcará can sell a partner company's tickets. Which fact on the component diagram answers it?
hint: What would the partner need to provide?

choices.text: Ticketing runs as three replicas, so it has spare capacity
choices.why: That is on the deployment diagram, and it is about load, not about partners.

choices.text: The passenger app requires Bookings from Ticketing
choices.why: True, and it is unchanged by a partner.

choices.text: Ticketing reaches pricing only through FareQuote
choices.why: Yes: the socket shows the only place the partner's fares have to plug in.

choices.text: The payment gateway is dashed
choices.why: It is external, which does not bear on where fares come from.

prompt: Which fact appears on Carcará's deployment diagram and on none of the other four?
hint: Something physical.

choices.text: That a booking owns its tickets, and they end with it
choices.why: That is a domain fact, from the class diagram.

choices.text: The station agent can do what a passenger does
choices.why: That is actor generalisation, on the use case diagram.

choices.text: Ticketing requires FareQuote
choices.why: That is an interface, on the component diagram.

choices.text: 300 phones each keep the day's tickets locally
choices.why: Right: where things physically are, and how many, is the deployment diagram's job.

prompt: Forty identical servers run the same service. How should a deployment diagram show them?
hint: What is the one fact the reader needs?

choices.text: Forty nodes, so the reader sees each one
choices.why: Forty boxes hide the one fact the reader needs among them: the number.

choices.text: One node and the count
choices.why: Yes: draw it once and write ×40.

choices.text: Drawn as a single component
choices.why: A component is logical; the servers are nodes.

choices.text: Leave them out, as they are identical
choices.why: The count is information operations needs.

prompt: Match each question to the UML diagram that answers it best.
hint: Look for who, and then, depends and where.

pairs.left: who uses the system, and for what?
what is a booking made of?
who waits for whom while paying?
could we replace the payment adapter?

prompt: Walking the purchase through the diagrams, Tainá finds the sequence shows Ticketing calling the Pricing database, while the component diagram shows Ticketing reaching Pricing only through FareQuote. What does the lesson say this was?
hint: Which one was wrong?

choices.text: A drawing error in the sequence diagram
choices.why: The sequence was drawn from what the code did, and it was right about that.

choices.text: A normal difference between logical and physical views
choices.why: The two views should agree about which interfaces are used; here they did not.

choices.text: A sign that component diagrams are not reliable
choices.why: The component diagram was the intended design; the code had drifted from it.

choices.text: A shortcut in the code from a past São João
choices.why: Yes: the disagreement between two views found a defect in the system itself.

prompt: Put the payment steps of Carcará's purchase in the order the sequence diagram shows.
hint: The seat comes before the money.
items: The API holds the seat for ten minutes
The API writes the booking as pending payment
The API asks the gateway to charge the card
The API marks the booking paid
trap: Charging before holding would let two passengers pay for the same seat.
